_rule: TIER 2 ONLY. This file carries what a manual needs and the graph does not: purpose, parts, procedure, known failures. It may NEVER restate a field the graph already declares — label, line, src, state, register, mig, or any relationship — because a second copy of those is a second truth. Sheets are addressed by node id and everything else is read from preview.html at run time. A work with no record here renders as a numbered, titled sheet stamped NOT YET WRITTEN. That is a legitimate state, and it is not to be filled with plausible text. See WORKS-MANUAL-SPEC §1 and §3.

sheets.purpose: To stop a teacher — human or machine — from explaining what the student already knows. The skill refuses to generate a course until it has established what the person in front of it can already do.

parts.name: trigger
parts.note: The request and a topic. Nothing is generated at this point, which is the whole departure from a normal prompt.

parts.name: diagnostic
parts.note: Closed questions only. This is the single load-bearing part; remove it and what remains is a generic course generator.

parts.name: level estimate
parts.note: One of five bands: beginner, familiar, intermediate, advanced, highly advanced.

parts.name: course
parts.note: Assembled upward from the estimate, so the starting point moves with the student rather than sitting at zero.

procedure: Receive the trigger and a topic. Do not generate a course yet.
Ask diagnostic questions relevant to the topic — yes/no and multiple choice only. Never open-ended, never a question the person answers by typing.
Establish current knowledge, prior exposure, practical experience, familiarity with foundational concepts, and where relevant the goal.
Place the answers on one of five bands: beginner, familiar, intermediate, advanced, highly advanced.
Build the course from that band upward. Do not assume the person knows nothing, and skip what they already hold.

knownFailures.name: Assumed ignorance
knownFailures.note: The failure this exists to prevent: teaching chapter one to someone who came for chapter nine. It is the default behaviour of every course generator that skips step 2.

knownFailures.name: The open question
knownFailures.note: Asking someone to state their own level returns a guess rather than a measurement — people under-state and over-state. The questions have to be answerable without self-assessment, which is why the constraint on question type is a rule and not a preference.

sheets.purpose: To put a way of thinking somewhere it can be walked through rather than described. The constraint that shapes everything else is that it must not be able to lie: a claim on the page has to come from a source the project holds, or it does not go on the page.

parts.name: the graph
parts.note: 143 declared objects and 126 relationships, extracted verbatim from the locked source at build time. It is never retyped, so the experience layer cannot disagree with the content it renders.

parts.name: the shell
parts.note: Markup, style, and the DOM structure. Delete the canvas and this still carries the whole mind — the 3D is an experience over the structure, not the structure itself.

parts.name: the renderer
parts.note: three.js r149, 594KB, inlined rather than linked. The artifact's content policy blocks every CDN, and a blocked script fails silently — so the library ships inside the file or the page dies without saying why.

parts.name: the scene
parts.note: The constellation, the fold from brain to universe, and the twelve charted planetary systems. Renders on demand: idle costs zero frames.

parts.name: the manual
parts.note: This. A second door off the same threshold, and the only part of the site that is deliberately not the mind.

procedure: Declare each thing once, in the locked source, with where it came from. Nothing is written twice.
Compose the artifact from the five parts above — one file, no external requests, nothing to fetch at run time.
Assert every claim against the live scene rather than against a copy of it, so a check cannot quietly agree with the thing it is checking.
Break each assertion on purpose. One that survives its own mutation is repaired; the mutation is never weakened to suit it.
Leave what is not yet documented visibly undocumented, and ship it in that state.

knownFailures.name: Every check passed while it was broken
knownFailures.note: Choosing a region from the closed mind flew the camera to where the region had been before the mind unfolded. Thirteen of fifteen landed completely off screen — one at y=2710, another at -6070,-38218 — and the entire suite passed throughout, because the checks run under reduced motion, where the fold completes before the framing is computed and the ordering that caused it cannot occur. A suite that only exercises one path proves things about one path.

knownFailures.name: The navigation was invisible
knownFailures.note: The fifteen region emblems are the only things to aim at in the menu, and they were being drawn dimmer than the constellation's own decorative stars — Philosophy at 45, Observation at 72, against background stars near 250. Choosing a region flew you into what looked like empty space. Nothing was broken; it was simply unlit.

knownFailures.name: An assertion went quiet
knownFailures.note: A check claimed to prove that hovering a region brightens it, but measured any rise at all across a wide window — and a hover also enlarges the point. With the brightening removed entirely, growth alone moved the reading from 62 to 64 and the check still passed. It now measures the core in a tight window, where growth spreads light outward and only emphasis raises it: +36% healthy against +0% mutated. A test that cannot fail is not a test.

knownFailures.name: The organ was built twice before it read as one
knownFailures.note: The first attempt drew evenly spaced curves across a closed shell and read as a helmet. The second was a lit mesh of 26,624 triangles, and was recognisable and wrong — a translucent clay organ, the object rather than the mind. Both were rejected outright rather than tuned.

parts.note: The only one with a folder of its own, and the only one whose argument is written down anywhere. It has its own sheet in this manual.

knownFailures.name: Six of seven cannot be chosen
knownFailures.note: A skill is reached for by its description — the model decides whether to use one by reading what it says it is for. Six of these say nothing beyond a filename, so nothing can reach for them on purpose and a stranger cannot tell what any of them does. The collection is a folder, not yet a set of tools.

knownFailures.name: The filename is the version
knownFailures.note: Two of the names carry a version and one carries a browser's duplicate-download suffix. Where the version lives in the filename there is no record of what changed between one and the next, and the earlier one is usually gone.

sheets.purpose: Three years of being paid by people who were watching the result. The through-line across both halves is the same habit: get next to whoever will actually use the thing before deciding what it should be, and keep asking them while it is being built.

parts.name: the freelance work
parts.note: Marketing, content, positioning, online presence, website design and proofreading, across multiple businesses and startups. Paid work for people measuring whether it worked.

parts.name: the defence startup
parts.note: A bootstrapped research and technology business building independent tech that does not depend on another country's. Its primary product is kamikaze drones for the Indian army — hitting a target from further away, so fewer people have to be near it.

parts.name: the people who use it
parts.note: Veteran and experienced soldiers, consulted before the design and present during it: they train with the team roughly six days a week. The customer is not researched at a distance; they are in the room.

parts.name: the constraints
parts.note: No budget, as a bootstrapped young startup, and nowhere to test — the team does not own dedicated land. Both shaped the work rather than merely slowing it.

procedure: Generate the idea, then go and check it rather than defending it.
Research the market, and treat that as the beginning of the question rather than the answer.
Consult veterans and experienced soldiers — people who have used something like it under the conditions it is actually for.
Work alongside them while it is being built, not once at the end. They are there roughly six days a week.
Take the feedback and iterate. Repeat until the people who will carry it stop finding fault with it.

knownFailures.name: Moved too fast to the pitch
knownFailures.note: An outreach to a startup founder went straight for the meeting, the pitch, the brainstorm, and the consultant framing. The founder answered: I am a spontaneous person, you just be by yourself, we will figure this out together if we are a great fit for each other. The lesson recorded at the time was two words — stop performing — and it is the exact opposite of the instinct that produced the message.

knownFailures.name: The first pitch explained instead of positioning
knownFailures.note: The original freelance pitch ran 54 words and spent its last sentence explaining why the reader should believe it. The refined version is 8 claims in 24 words and explains nothing. The principle it was rewritten against: show relevance, demonstrate understanding, then ask for the opportunity — and avoid generic consultant language, which is what the first version was made of.

knownFailures.name: Nowhere to test
knownFailures.note: Not owning land is not a problem that can be engineered around, and it is recorded as a constraint rather than solved. Some limits are conditions of the work, and the honest thing is to name them instead of implying they were overcome.

authority: Siddhesh, 2026-09-02 — the description of the project, supplied in full and quoted rather than summarised
sheets.purpose: To find a random-number generator faster than the one securing most of the internet, that needs no special chip to run. Speed alone is not the test: a candidate has to be enough better to be worth changing something almost everything depends on.

parts.name: the incumbent
parts.note: The generator securing most of the internet — the thing any candidate has to beat. Which one it is is not stated here.

parts.name: the constraint
parts.note: No special chip. A candidate that needs particular hardware to be fast does not count, however fast it is on that hardware.

parts.name: the candidate
parts.note: After months of testing, one is 3% faster — and carries the first real evidence that it might be genuinely stronger per unit of work, not merely quicker.

knownFailures.name: 3% is not enough
knownFailures.note: Nobody replaces the thing securing most of the internet for 3%. A margin has to be worth the cost and risk of changing it, and this one is not, so the result is a real finding and not yet a reason to switch. The hunt continues.
